issues.legal_issue: The description of a spouse as the owner of property in a will may confer only a life estate when the will as a whole shows that the testator intended the property to pass absolutely to another beneficiary after the spouse’s death.
material_facts: The testator’s will described his wife as owner of his entire estate after his death and gave her proprietary powers, but did not expressly give her the power to make transfers of all kinds.

The will expressly gave the later beneficiary the power to make transfers of all kinds after the wife’s death, and provided that the beneficiary would take absolutely if the wife died before the testator.
The testator described the beneficiary as his heir, directed that the beneficiary serve the wife, and provided that future property would pass to them on the same stated conditions.
The will recited the testator’s concern that his brother and nephew might trouble his wife and the beneficiary, and the testator did not intend his property to pass to those relatives.
The wife later made a gift and a will concerning some of the property in favour of the appellant.
issues.conclusion: The will gave the wife only a life estate and gave the later beneficiary an absolute estate after her death. The wife’s gift and will in favour of the appellant therefore failed, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: A will must be construed by ascertaining intention from its words, read as a whole and in light of the circumstances, the testator’s position and family relationships; effect should, where legally possible, be given to every disposition and expression, and apparently conflicting provisions should be reconciled where possible. The word “malik” ordinarily describes an owner with full proprietary rights, including alienation, but context and surrounding circumstances may show that full rights were not intended. The Court relied on Ram Gopal v. Nand Lal; Venkata Narasimha v. Parthasarathy; Gnanambal Ammal v. T. Raju Ayyar; Raj Bajrang Bahadur Singh v. Thakurain Bakhtraj Kuer; Pearey Lal v. Rameshwar Das; Ramachandra Shenoy v. Mrs. Hilda Brite; Sasiman Chowdhurain v. Shib Narayan Chowdhury; Musammat Surajmani v. Rabi Nath Ojha; Krishna Biharilal v. Gulabchand; and Dhyan Singh v. Jugal Kishore.

rule.if: will_construction_proceeding and will_gives_spouse_property_after_testator_death and will_names_later_beneficiary_after_spouse and will_gives_later_beneficiary_transfer_power_but_not_spouse and will_shows_intent_to_keep_property_from_testators_heirs

predicates.will_construction_proceeding: A court was asked to determine the effect of a testamentary instrument.
predicates.will_gives_spouse_property_after_testato: The testator’s will gives the spouse property to enjoy after the testator’s death.
predicates.will_names_later_beneficiary_after_spous: The will provides that another beneficiary is to take the property after the spouse’s death.
predicates.will_gives_later_beneficiary_transfer_po: The will expressly gives the later beneficiary power to transfer the property but does not expressly give that power to the spouse.
predicates.will_shows_intent_to_keep_property_from_: The will indicates that the testator wanted to prevent the testator’s own relatives from inheriting the property.

issues.definition: When a court construing a will finds that it gives property to a spouse, names a later beneficiary, expressly gives transfer power to that beneficiary but not the spouse, and shows an intention to keep the property from the testator’s heirs, the spouse has a life estate and the later beneficiary takes absolutely.
